unit_description: This unit covers measurement and line plots. Students choose and estimate customary length units, measure to the nearest quarter inch, choose units for weight, mass, and liquid volume, and create and interpret line plots including fractional data.
unit_goals: Choose and estimate customary length units.
Measure to the nearest quarter inch.
Choose units for weight, mass, and liquid volume.
Create and interpret line plots, including fractional data.
Use measurement data to answer questions.

weeks.weekly_focus: Students practice measuring lengths, choosing appropriate units, and representing measurement data on line plots.

lessons.lesson_title: Choose and Estimate Customary Length Units
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by estimating lengths of classroom objects in inches, feet, and yards.
lessons.concept: Different units are used for different lengths. Use inches for short objects, feet for medium objects, and yards for longer distances. Estimate before measuring.
lessons.practice: Choose the best customary unit and estimate lengths.
lessons.objective: Choose and estimate customary length units.

questions.prompt: Which is better for measuring a pencil: inches or yards?
Which is better for measuring a room: feet or inches?
questions.hint: A room is longer than a few inches.

questions.prompt: Estimate the length of a pencil in inches.
questions.hint: A typical pencil is about 6 inches.

learn.title: Choose and Estimate Customary Length Units
teaching_points: Yards for long lengths or distances.

example.prompt: What unit would you use to measure the length of a school bus?

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: What unit would you use to measure the width of a book?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Choose the best unit and estimate the length for each object.

bigIdea.title: Choose and Estimate Customary Length Units
bigIdea.subtitle: Pick the right tool for the length
bigIdea.intro: You would not measure a pencil in yards. Choose a unit that makes sense for the length of the object. Inches, feet, and yards each have a best use.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: When is it better to measure in feet instead of inches?

ruleCards.description: Use inches for things shorter than a hand.
Use feet for things taller or longer than a few inches.

lessons.lesson_title: Measure to the Nearest Quarter Inch
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by measuring objects with a ruler marked in inches and half inches.
lessons.concept: A ruler can be divided into fourths of an inch. Measure to the nearest quarter inch by finding the closest 1/4, 1/2, or 3/4 mark.
lessons.practice: Measure lengths to the nearest quarter inch.
lessons.objective: Measure to the nearest quarter inch.

questions.prompt: How many quarter inches are in one inch?
A line ends halfway between 2 and 3 inches. What is the nearest half inch?
A pencil ends at the first mark after 3 inches. What is its length?

learn.title: Measure to the Nearest Quarter Inch
teaching_points: An inch is divided into 4 equal parts.
The marks are 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of an inch.
Find the closest mark to the end of the object.

example.prompt: Measure a pencil that ends at the 3/4 mark after 5 inches.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: A crayon ends halfway between 4 and 4 1/2 inches. What is the nearest quarter inch?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Measure each object to the nearest quarter inch.

flashcards.title: Quarter Inches
flashcards.instructions: Review measuring to the nearest quarter inch.

bigIdea.title: Measure to the Nearest Quarter Inch
bigIdea.subtitle: Use the closest mark
bigIdea.intro: Rulers are divided into fourths of an inch. Find the closest quarter-inch mark to the end of the object. This gives a measurement to the nearest quarter inch.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: How do you know which quarter-inch mark is closest?

ruleCards.description: An inch is divided into four equal parts.
Find the quarter-inch mark closest to the end of the object.

lessons.lesson_title: Choose Units for Weight, Mass, and Liquid Volume
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by matching objects to units of grams, kilograms, ounces, pounds, liters, and milliliters.
lessons.concept: Weight and mass can be measured in grams, kilograms, ounces, or pounds. Liquid volume is measured in liters or milliliters. Choose the unit that matches the size of the object or amount.
lessons.practice: Choose the best unit for weight, mass, and liquid volume.
lessons.objective: Choose units for weight, mass, and liquid volume.

warmup.title: Luma Charge
warmup.instructions: Warm up with weight, mass, and volume units.

questions.prompt: Which is better for measuring a bottle of water: liters or milliliters?
Which is better for measuring a pumpkin: ounces or pounds?
Which is better for a paper clip: grams or kilograms?
questions.hint: A paper clip is very light.

learn.title: Choose Units for Weight, Mass, and Liquid Volume
teaching_points: Use small units for small amounts.
Use large units for large amounts.
Match the unit to the object's size.

example.prompt: What unit would you use for the mass of a book?

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: What unit would you use for the liquid volume of a small medicine cup?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Choose the best unit for measuring each item.

flashcards.title: Weight, Mass, Volume Units
flashcards.instructions: Review units for weight, mass, and volume.

bigIdea.title: Choose Units for Weight, Mass, and Liquid Volume
bigIdea.subtitle: Match the unit to the amount
bigIdea.intro: Just like length, weight, mass, and volume need the right unit. Use grams or ounces for small things, kilograms or pounds for heavier things, and milliliters or liters for liquids depending on the amount.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: When would you use milliliters instead of liters?

ruleCards.description: Use grams for small or light objects.
Use liters for larger amounts of liquid.

lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by organizing a set of measurements on a number line.
lessons.concept: A line plot shows data as marks above a number line. Each mark stands for one measurement. Use line plots to show measurement data, including fractions.
lessons.practice: Create and interpret line plots with whole-number and fractional data.
lessons.objective: Create and interpret line plots, including fractional data.

questions.prompt: A line plot shows X marks above 3/4 and 1. How many measurements are 3/4?
On a line plot, what does each X stand for?
questions.hint: Each X is one data point.

questions.prompt: Measurements: 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4. How many Xs go above 3?

learn.title: Create and Interpret Line Plots
teaching_points: Draw a number line with the measurements.
Place an X above each measurement.

example.prompt: Create a line plot for these measurements: 1/2, 1/2, 3/4, 3/4, 3/4, 1.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: Create a line plot for: 1/4, 1/2, 1/2, 3/4, 1, 1. How many measurements are 1/2?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Create and answer questions about each line plot.

bigIdea.title: Create and Interpret Line Plots
bigIdea.subtitle: Mark data on a number line
bigIdea.intro: A line plot is like a number line that shows data. Put an X above each measurement. You can use line plots to see which measurements are most common and answer questions about the data.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: What does each X on a line plot represent?

ruleCards.description: The number line shows all possible measurements.
Each X stands for one data value.

lessons.fact_drill: Rapid review of choosing length units, measuring to quarter inches, choosing weight/mass/volume units, and line plots.
lessons.concept: Review the four big ideas from this unit: customary length units, measuring to the nearest quarter inch, choosing units for weight/mass/volume, and creating and interpreting line plots.
lessons.practice: Complete a balanced evaluation covering the skills from this unit.
lessons.objective: Show what you know about measurement data.

warmup.title: Luma Charge
warmup.instructions: Get ready to show what you know.

questions.prompt: Measure to the nearest quarter inch: a crayon at the 3/4 mark after 4 inches.
Which unit is best for the mass of a backpack: grams or kilograms?
A line plot has 4 Xs above 2 and 1 X above 3. How many total measurements?

learn.title: Ready to Show What You Know
teaching_points: Use any strategy that helps you.

example.prompt: You have learned four big ideas this unit.
example.equation: length units + quarter inches + weight/mass/volume + line plots = measurement data

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: Which unit is best for the length of a school hallway: inches, feet, or yards?

practice_block.title: Unit Evaluation
practice_block.instructions: Answer all questions carefully to show your understanding.

flashcards.title: Unit 34 Review
flashcards.instructions: Review key terms from Unit 34 before the evaluation.

bigIdea.title: Unit Evaluation: Measurement Data
bigIdea.subtitle: Show what you know
bigIdea.intro: This evaluation checks your understanding of the four big ideas from this unit: choosing customary length units, measuring to the nearest quarter inch, choosing units for weight/mass/liquid volume, and creating and interpreting line plots.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: What do you know about measurement and line plots?

ruleCards.equation: match the unit to the object
ruleCards.description: Choose a unit that makes sense for the size.
Each X stands for one data point on the number line.
